name: slots.courseSpecifics
description: This is a master's course whose students come from very different bachelor's degrees: a physicist and a political scientist sit side by side. Do not assume the student has the natural science, the social science or the humanities background; find out which they have, pitch the explanation to it, and use the student's own discipline as a bridge into the unfamiliar one. Every node is examined in a transdisciplinary setting, so wherever it fits, ask how the same question looks from one of the other two perspectives. Use European and Nordic examples where they serve, alongside global ones. Numbers on the climate should follow the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report; say so when you cite one, and say when a figure has been updated since.

name: System and system boundary
description:
System: a set of elements connected so that together they produce behaviour that none of them produces alone.
System boundary: the line the analyst draws between what is inside the system and what is treated as its environment.

name: Stock and flow
description:
Stock: a quantity that accumulates over time, such as CO2 in the atmosphere or money in an account.
Flow: a rate that adds to or drains a stock, such as annual emissions or annual uptake by the ocean.

name: Feedback loop
description:
Reinforcing feedback: a loop in which a change sets off further change in the same direction.
Balancing feedback: a loop that counteracts a change and pulls the system back towards a state.

name: Reason about a stock from its flows
description: explain why a stock keeps rising while its inflow falls, for as long as the inflow is larger than the outflow, and apply that to atmospheric CO2 when emissions are cut but not to zero.

name: Draw a causal loop diagram
description: draw a causal loop diagram of an environmental problem, mark the polarity of each link, and label each loop as reinforcing or balancing.

name: Tipping point and hysteresis
description:
Tipping point: a threshold beyond which a small change sets off a self-reinforcing shift of the system into a different state.
Hysteresis: the system does not return to its old state when the driver is brought back below the threshold.

name: Wicked problem
description: Wicked problem: a problem with no definitive formulation and no stopping rule, where every attempted solution changes the problem and the stakeholders disagree about what the problem is.

name: Leverage point
description: Leverage point: a place in a system where an intervention changes the behaviour of the whole system. Changing a goal or a paradigm usually moves more than changing a parameter such as a price or a quota.

name: Identify leverage points in a system
description: identify possible interventions in a causal loop diagram, rank them from shallow (parameters) to deep (rules, goals, paradigms), and argue which one is worth pursuing.

name: Weather and climate
description:
Weather: the state of the atmosphere at a given place and time.
Climate: the statistics of weather over a long period, conventionally 30 years, including its averages, variability and extremes.

name: Earth's energy balance and albedo
description:
Earth's energy balance: the balance between incoming shortwave radiation from the Sun and outgoing longwave radiation from Earth; a lasting imbalance changes the temperature.
Albedo: the fraction of incoming sunlight a surface reflects.

name: Greenhouse effect
description: Greenhouse effect: gases such as water vapour, CO2 and methane absorb longwave radiation emitted by the surface and re-emit it, partly back down, so the surface is warmer than it would be without them.

name: Radiative forcing
description: Radiative forcing: the change in Earth's energy balance caused by a driver such as added CO2 or aerosols, measured in W/m². Positive forcing warms, negative forcing cools.

name: Carbon cycle and carbon sink
description:
Carbon cycle: the exchange of carbon among the atmosphere, the ocean, the land biosphere and rock, on time scales from years to millions of years.
Carbon sink: a reservoir that takes up more carbon than it releases, such as the ocean today.

name: Equilibrium climate sensitivity
description: Equilibrium climate sensitivity: the long-term global warming that follows a doubling of the CO2 concentration, once the climate system has adjusted.

name: Explain the main climate feedbacks
description: explain the water vapour, ice–albedo, cloud and permafrost carbon feedbacks, and say for each whether it amplifies or dampens warming and how certain that is.

name: Key numbers of the climate
description:
CO2 concentration before industrialisation: about 280 ppm
CO2 concentration in 2024: about 424 ppm
global warming 2011–2020 relative to 1850–1900 (IPCC AR6): about 1.1 °C
likely range of equilibrium climate sensitivity (IPCC AR6): 2.5–4 °C
global CO2 emissions per year, including land use: about 40 Gt CO2
fraction of human CO2 emissions that stays in the atmosphere: about half
temperature goal of the Paris Agreement: well below 2 °C, pursuing 1.5 °C

name: Remaining carbon budget
description: Remaining carbon budget: the cumulative CO2 that can still be emitted while keeping a given probability of staying below a given warming level. It exists because warming is roughly proportional to cumulative CO2 emissions.

name: Estimate the years left in a carbon budget
description: estimate how many years of current emissions fit within a remaining carbon budget, and explain what the answer does and does not tell us about when emissions must reach net zero.

name: Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP)
description: Shared Socioeconomic Pathway: a storyline of how population, economy, technology and policy may develop, combined with a forcing level in names such as SSP2-4.5 (a middle-of-the-road world reaching 4.5 W/m² by 2100).

name: Read a climate projection
description: read a scenario figure from the IPCC, and separate the three sources of spread in it: the choice of scenario, differences between models, and natural variability.

name: Explain how warming changes extremes and sea level
description: explain how warming changes heat extremes, heavy rainfall, drought, sea level and ocean acidity, separating what has been observed from what is projected.

name: Assess a climate tipping element
description: assess a climate tipping element, such as the Greenland ice sheet, the Atlantic overturning circulation or the Amazon rainforest: which feedback drives it, at roughly what warming it may be crossed, and how fast and how reversibly it would change.

name: Energy and power
description:
Energy: the capacity to do work, measured in joules or kilowatt-hours (kWh).
Power: the rate at which energy is converted, measured in watts (W). A power plant has a power; a year of its output is an amount of energy.

name: Primary, final and useful energy
description:
Primary energy: energy as found in nature, before conversion, such as coal, wind or sunlight.
Final energy: energy delivered to the user, such as electricity or petrol.
Useful energy: what is left as heat, light or motion after the last conversion.

name: Calculate the efficiency of a conversion chain
description: calculate the overall efficiency of a chain of energy conversions, from primary to useful energy, and say where the largest losses are.

name: Carbon intensity and life-cycle emissions
description:
Carbon intensity: emissions per unit of energy, for electricity usually given in g CO2-eq/kWh.
Life-cycle emissions: emissions over the whole life of a technology, from mining and manufacture through operation to decommissioning.

name: Decompose emissions with the Kaya identity
description: decompose a country's CO2 emissions into population × GDP per person × energy per unit of GDP × CO2 per unit of energy, and say which factor a given policy acts on.

name: Variable renewables and capacity factor
description:
Variable renewable energy: electricity from sources whose output follows the weather, such as wind and solar.
Capacity factor: the actual output over a year divided by what the plant would produce running at full power all year.
Dispatchable source: one whose output can be raised or lowered on demand, such as hydropower with a reservoir.

name: Explain how a power system balances variable supply
description: explain how a power system with much wind and solar keeps supply equal to demand at every moment, using storage, demand response, transmission and dispatchable capacity.

name: Levelised cost of electricity (LCOE)
description: Levelised cost of electricity: the total lifetime cost of a power plant divided by its total lifetime output, which lets technologies with different cost profiles be compared per kWh.

name: Compare energy sources across criteria
description: compare two energy sources on life-cycle emissions, cost, land and material use, reliability and social acceptance, stating the system boundary used for each number.

name: Energy transition and electrification
description:
Energy transition: a lasting shift of an energy system from one dominant set of sources and technologies to another, today from fossil fuels to low-carbon sources.
Electrification: replacing direct fuel use, as in cars and heating, with electricity.

name: Rebound effect
description: Rebound effect: the part of an expected energy saving that is lost because greater efficiency makes energy services cheaper, so people use more of them. When use rises by more than the saving, it is called the Jevons paradox.

name: Ecosystem and ecosystem services
description:
Ecosystem: a community of organisms together with its physical environment, linked by flows of energy and matter.
Ecosystem services: the benefits people draw from ecosystems, such as food, pollination, clean water and climate regulation.

name: Biodiversity
description: Biodiversity: the variety of life at three levels: genetic variation within species, the variety of species, and the variety of ecosystems.

name: Resilience and regime shift
description:
Resilience: the capacity of a system to absorb disturbance and reorganise while keeping its essential function and structure.
Regime shift: a large, lasting change in the structure and function of an ecosystem, such as a clear lake turning turbid.

name: Planetary boundaries
description: Planetary boundaries: limits for nine Earth-system processes, among them climate change, biosphere integrity, land-system change and biogeochemical flows, which together mark a safe operating space for humanity.

name: Use the planetary boundaries framework on a case
description: use the planetary boundaries framework to assess the pressures from an activity or a sector, and point out what the framework cannot say about local impacts and about who causes the pressure.

name: Explain how land use links climate and biodiversity
description: explain how land use connects climate change and biodiversity loss: deforestation as a source of emissions, land as a carbon sink, and the trade-offs of bioenergy and tree planting.

name: Analyse a water–energy–food trade-off
description: analyse a case where water, energy and food compete, such as hydropower and irrigation in one river basin, and show how an improvement in one sector creates pressure in another.

name: Common-pool resource and tragedy of the commons
description:
Common-pool resource: a resource it is hard to exclude people from, and where one person's use reduces what is left for others, such as a fishery or the atmosphere as a dump for CO2.
Tragedy of the commons: overuse of such a resource when each user gains from using more while the cost is shared by all.

name: Polycentric governance
description: Polycentric governance: many overlapping centres of decision-making at different scales, each with some autonomy, as opposed to one central authority. Ostrom showed that communities often govern commons well this way.

name: Mitigation and adaptation
description:
Mitigation: reducing emissions or increasing sinks, so that less climate change happens.
Adaptation: adjusting society and ecosystems to the climate change that does happen.

name: Paris Agreement and NDC
description:
Paris Agreement: the 2015 UN climate treaty, which aims to keep warming well below 2 °C and to pursue 1.5 °C, and in which every party sets its own targets.
Nationally determined contribution (NDC): a country's own climate pledge under the agreement, to be updated every five years with rising ambition.

name: Multilevel governance
description: Multilevel governance: decision-making spread across global, regional (such as the EU), national and local levels, and shared with non-state actors such as companies, cities and NGOs.

name: Assess a country's climate pledge
description: assess whether a country's NDC is consistent with the Paris temperature goal, using a carbon budget and an independent tracker, and state the fairness assumptions behind the verdict.

name: Map stakeholders by interest and influence
description: map the stakeholders in an environmental conflict by their interest and their influence, and say whose voices are missing from the map.

name: Analyse a governance case
description: analyse a real climate or environmental decision: who decided, at which level, with what legitimacy and under what pressure, and what would have had to change for a different outcome.

name: Externality
description: Externality: a cost or benefit of an activity that falls on someone who is not party to it and is not reflected in its price. Greenhouse gas emissions are a negative externality.

name: Discount rate and present value
description:
Present value: what a future cost or benefit is worth today.
Discount rate: the yearly rate by which future values are reduced to present value; a high rate makes far-future damages count for little.

name: Social cost of carbon
description: Social cost of carbon: the present value of all future damages caused by emitting one more tonne of CO2. The estimate depends strongly on the discount rate and on how damages are valued.

name: Calculate present value at different discount rates
description: calculate the present value of a climate damage occurring 50 or 100 years from now at several discount rates, and explain why choosing the rate is partly an ethical decision.

name: Carbon tax and emissions trading
description:
Carbon tax: a price per tonne of emissions, set by the government, which leaves the quantity to the market.
Emissions trading (cap and trade): a cap on total emissions with tradable permits, which leaves the price to the market, as in the EU ETS.

name: Compare climate policy instruments
description: compare a carbon tax, emissions trading and direct regulation on certainty of price and of quantity, cost-effectiveness, revenue, distributional effects and political feasibility.

name: Decoupling, green growth and degrowth
description:
Decoupling: economic growth without a matching growth in emissions or resource use; relative decoupling when emissions grow more slowly than GDP, absolute when they fall while GDP grows.
Green growth: the position that absolute decoupling can be fast enough.
Degrowth: the position that rich countries must reduce material throughput, and with it probably GDP.

name: Weigh the evidence in the growth debate
description: weigh the evidence on whether absolute decoupling is happening fast enough, using emissions and GDP data for a few countries, and say what each side would have to show to convince the other.

name: Climate justice
description:
Climate justice: the demand that the burdens and benefits of climate change and climate policy are shared fairly.
Distributive justice: who bears costs and receives benefits.
Procedural justice: who takes part in the decisions.
Recognition justice: whose identities, knowledge and values are acknowledged.

name: Intergenerational justice
description: Intergenerational justice: what the people alive today owe to future generations, who will live with the consequences of today's emissions but have no say in them.

name: Common but differentiated responsibilities
description: Common but differentiated responsibilities: the principle in the UN climate regime that all countries share responsibility for climate change, but in proportion to their contribution and their capacity to act.

name: Compare measures of responsibility for emissions
description: compare a country's responsibility measured by annual, per-person, cumulative historical and consumption-based emissions, and show how the ranking of countries changes with the measure.

name: Just transition
description: Just transition: an energy transition carried out so that workers, communities and regions dependent on fossil fuels are not left to carry its costs alone.

name: Build and defend an ethical argument on a climate question
description: build an argument on a climate question, such as who should pay for loss and damage, state which ethical principle it rests on, and answer the strongest objection to it.

name: Anthropocene
description: Anthropocene: the proposed name for an epoch in which human activity is a dominant force on the Earth system. The term is contested both on geological grounds and because it names humanity as a whole rather than particular economies and actors.

name: Great Acceleration
description: Great Acceleration: the sharp and simultaneous rise, from about 1950, in human activity (population, energy use, GDP, fertiliser use) and in pressure on the Earth system (CO2, biodiversity loss, nitrogen).

name: Milestones of environmental governance
description:
UN Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm: 1972
Brundtland report, Our Common Future: 1987
Montreal Protocol on the ozone layer: 1987
IPCC founded: 1988
Rio Earth Summit and the UNFCCC: 1992
Kyoto Protocol: 1997
Paris Agreement: 2015
UN Sustainable Development Goals adopted: 2015

name: Framing and narrative
description:
Frame: the way a text selects and emphasises some aspects of an issue, which suggests what the problem is, who is responsible and what should be done.
Narrative: a story with actors, a sequence of events and a moral, through which people make sense of an issue such as climate change.

name: Analyse how a text frames climate change
description: analyse how a news article, an advertisement or a policy document frames climate change, such as crisis, opportunity, security threat or hoax, and say which actions the frame makes thinkable and which it hides.

name: Trace how an environmental problem became a problem
description: trace how an environmental problem, such as acid rain in Scandinavia or the ozone hole, came to be recognised, contested and acted on, and draw one lesson for climate change and one way the cases differ.

name: Indigenous and local knowledge
description: Indigenous and local knowledge: knowledge about land, water, animals and weather built up over generations of practice by a community, such as Sámi reindeer herders' knowledge of snow and grazing, which can complement scientific observation and which has its own ways of being validated.

name: Multi-, inter- and transdisciplinarity
description:
Multidisciplinary: several disciplines work side by side on a topic, each with its own questions and methods.
Interdisciplinary: disciplines integrate their concepts and methods into a shared analysis.
Transdisciplinary: researchers and societal actors frame the problem and produce the knowledge together, crossing the line between science and society.

name: Epistemology and standards of evidence
description: Epistemology: the study of what counts as knowledge and how it is justified. Disciplines differ in what they accept as evidence, from a controlled measurement to an interview to the reading of a text, and in what they mean by a valid result.

name: Knowledge co-production
description: Knowledge co-production: a research process in which scientists and non-academic actors, such as municipalities, firms or residents, take part in framing the question, producing the knowledge and using it.

name: Positionality and reflexivity
description:
Positionality: the researcher's own background, values and position in relation to the people and the problem studied.
Reflexivity: the practice of examining how that position shapes the questions asked, the data gathered and the conclusions drawn.

name: Formulate a research question with societal partners
description: formulate a research question on a sustainability problem together with societal partners, so that it is both researchable and useful to them, and say what each side brings to it.

name: Plan a participatory method
description: choose and plan a participatory method, such as a stakeholder workshop, scenario building or citizen science, for a given question, and say how its results will feed back to the participants.

name: Translate a concept between disciplines
description: explain what a word such as 'risk', 'resilience' or 'value' means in a natural science, in a social science and in the humanities, and show how a team goes wrong when it assumes the meanings are the same.

name: Communicate findings to different audiences
description: present the same finding on climate, energy or environment to a scientific audience, to a policy-maker and to the public, choosing a different frame, level of detail and handling of uncertainty for each.

name: Analyse a climate–energy–environment case transdisciplinarily
description: analyse a real case, such as a planned wind farm on reindeer grazing land, by combining a systems map, the natural science of its impacts, the governance and economics of the decision and its ethical and cultural dimensions, and propose a way forward that the stakeholders could accept.
